strengths: Rigorous and comprehensive theoretical development connecting SU(2) matrices, stereographic projection, and Möbius transformations to Wahba's problem, with detailed proofs provided in supplementary material.

Derives multiple new closed-form/linear-constraint formulations of Wahba's problem (stereographic plane, 3D sphere, Möbius approximation) that recover known optimal solutions (matching Davenport's Q-method), demonstrating internal consistency.

Provides efficient closed-form solutions for the 1-point and 2-point minimal cases with systematic handling of singular/degenerate configurations, and shows modest computational efficiency gains (fewer multiplications) versus existing two-point solvers (QUEST, Fast Quat).

Introduces two new higher-dimensional rotation representations for neural network learning (2-vec and QuadMobius variants) motivated by the theoretical results, including derivation of custom backpropagation formulas through eigendecomposition/SVD operations.

Reasonably thorough experimental validation: large-scale synthetic trials (1M) for Wahba solvers, systematic ablations over learning rates/losses/dimensions for the learning task, and an additional real-image (NeRF) camera orientation experiment.
Good transparency/reproducibility effort: full derivations, additional results, and timing data included in supplementary material.
weaknesses: The core Wahba's-problem solutions (GP, GS) are shown to exactly reproduce existing optimal solvers (e.g., Q-method), so the main contribution here is a reformulation/alternative derivation rather than a new algorithmic capability or accuracy improvement; practical efficiency gains reported are modest and only for special minimal cases.

The proposed learning representations (2-vec, QuadMobiusAlg/SVD) show only small, inconsistent improvements over existing strong baselines (QCQP, SVD-based) in Table 3/6, with no statistical significance analysis, making it hard to conclude a genuine advantage; results across many trials in the supplementary table are very close between representations.

The real-world vision experiment (Sec. 5.3) is very limited in scope: a single NeRF synthetic scene, small dataset, and the authors themselves note the test-set results are mixed and correlate weakly with validation results, with possible overfitting, undermining the practical significance claim.

Novelty of the deep-learning representations is somewhat incremental, being explicitly derived as combinations/extensions of prior work ([8, 21, 26]), rather than a fundamentally new learning paradigm.
The paper is extremely dense and notation-heavy (many equations, projective/complex constructs), which may hinder accessibility and broader impact despite being technically correct.

The 3D sphere solution (GS) offering no accuracy advantage over standard methods and only being algebraically distinct raises the question of what concrete benefit the SU(2) framing provides beyond conceptual insight, since eigendecomposition is still required in the general case.
Limited discussion of scalability or applicability of the proposed methods to larger, real-world attitude/pose estimation systems beyond the small-scale synthetic and single-scene experiments.

strengths: Mathematically rigorous treatment connecting SU(2)/Möbius transformations to Wahba's problem, with extensive proofs provided in the supplementary material.

The two-point closed-form solvers (Sec. 3) offer a modest but real computational efficiency improvement (fewer multiplications) over existing closed-form methods like QUEST and Fast Quaternion, with careful handling of degenerate/singular cases.

Reasonably comprehensive experimental protocol: synthetic Wahba's problem trials at multiple noise levels and point counts, a learning-based rotation regression comparison against several established representations (Euler, Quaternion, Gram-Schmidt, QCQP, SVD), and a real vision task on NeRF-synthetic images.
Careful bookkeeping of backpropagation derivatives for the proposed complex-valued learned representations (Appendix B), supporting reproducibility of the learning experiments.
weaknesses: The core theoretical contribution (Sec. 2) is essentially a re-derivation of known Wahba's-problem solutions through an isomorphic (SU(2)/quaternion) lens; the paper's own experiments (Tables 1 and 5) confirm the proposed GP and GS solvers produce numerically identical results to Davenport's Q-method and other decades-old algorithms, indicating limited new estimation capability rather than a genuinely new method.

The practical efficiency gain from the two-point solver (Table 2) is incremental (roughly 2-3x fewer multiplications in the unweighted case) and not clearly impactful for typical applications where such savings are unlikely to be a bottleneck.

For the learning-representation contributions (2-vec, QuadMobius), improvements over existing strong baselines (QCQP, SVD) are marginal and inconsistent across configurations (Table 6 shows no representation consistently dominates across the 24 trial settings), undermining claims of a clear advantage.

The camera orientation vision experiment (Table 4) shows mixed and weakly-correlated validation/test results, with the authors themselves attributing this to possible overfitting; no representation is convincingly best, weakening the practical significance claim.

The QuadMobius representation requires substantially higher output dimensionality (16D) and computational cost (Table 7 shows it is 2-3x slower in both training and inference than SVD/QCQP) for at-best marginal accuracy gains, raising questions about its practical value.

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed variance reporting is provided for the learning experiments, making it hard to assess whether the small differences between top representations are meaningful or noise.
The real-world vision evaluation is limited to a single small dataset (NeRF synthetic lego) with a lightweight backbone, providing weak evidence of applicability beyond synthetic benchmarks.

The paper's stated motivation (SU(2) is underexplored in robotics/vision) is not strongly substantiated by outcomes that meaningfully outperform existing SO(3)/quaternion-based approaches, so the practical significance of the SU(2) perspective remains unclear despite its mathematical elegance.

strengths: The paper provides a rigorous, well-developed theoretical framework connecting special unitary matrices (SU(2)), stereographic/Möbius transformations, and Wahba's problem, with detailed proofs in the supplementary material.

Derives new closed-form solutions for one-point and two-point (noiseless and general) cases that are more computationally efficient (fewer multiplications/operations) than existing methods (Table 2), which is a nice practical contribution for attitude estimation.

Introduces two new higher-dimensional rotation representations for neural network learning (2-vec and QuadMobius), motivated directly by the theoretical derivations, showing conceptual coherence between the theory and application sections.

Experimental validation is fairly comprehensive: synthetic Wahba's problem benchmarks against many established solvers (Q-method, QUEST, ESOQ2, FLAE, OLAE), a learning-based rotation regression task replicating prior work (SVD, QCQP, Gram-Schmidt baselines), and a real-world camera orientation estimation task on NeRF images.

Provides careful treatment of degenerate/singular cases (e.g., vanishing cross products, points at infinity) which are often glossed over in related literature, along with systematic strategies for numerically robust implementations.
Derivatives for backpropagation through eigendecomposition and SVD-based mappings are explicitly derived and validated against automatic differentiation, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core Wahba's problem solutions (GP, GS) are shown to be numerically equivalent to existing optimal solvers (Table 1), so the primary novelty is the derivation pathway rather than new empirical capability or performance gains.

Learning-representation experiments show only modest and inconsistent improvements over existing strong baselines (QCQP, SVD); the authors themselves note results are 'mixed' on the camera orientation test set and correlate weakly with validation performance, suggesting possible overfitting or limited robustness of the claimed advantage.

The QuadMobius representations are computationally more expensive than SVD/QCQP (Table 7) due to complex arithmetic, yet do not show a clear, consistent accuracy advantage that would justify this cost in practice.

Real-world validation is limited to a single dataset (NeRF synthetic 'lego') with a fairly narrow experimental setup (single backbone, limited scene diversity), limiting confidence in generalizability of the learning representations.

The paper is dense and mathematically heavy, and the broader practical significance/impact of adopting SU(2)-based representations over well-established quaternion/SVD-based approaches is not strongly argued beyond efficiency in narrow minimal-case scenarios.

Ablations on why QuadMobiusAlg and QuadMobiusSVD (mathematically equivalent) produce different practical results are inconclusive ('unclear in which cases each might excel'), leaving open questions about robustness and choice of implementation in practice.

strengths: Provides a rigorous and fairly comprehensive theoretical reformulation of Wahba's problem using SU(2)/complex projective geometry, deriving linear quaternion constraints from three different parameterizations (stereographic, Mobius approximation, 3D sphere) with full proofs in the appendix.

Derives several practically useful byproducts: efficient residual computation for iterative solvers, simplified constrained optimization with axis priors (e.g., IMU gravity vector) without needing intermediate coordinate frames, and new closed-form two-point Wahba solutions that reduce multiplication counts (especially the unweighted case) versus existing closed-form solvers (Markley 2002, Shuster & Oh 1981).

Introduces two new continuous rotation representations (2-vec and QuadMobius) motivated directly from the theoretical results, with detailed derivations, backpropagation formulas for the SVD/eigendecomposition steps, and reasonably broad empirical evaluation across three distinct benchmarks (ModelNet10-SO3 shape alignment, unsupervised inverse kinematics, and camera pose regression).

Extensive supplementary analysis, including gradient-balance comparisons between 2-vec and Gram-Schmidt, dropout/robustness ablations and gradient-magnitude studies for QuadMobius, timing benchmarks, and a large synthetic learning study (24 trials) varying loss type, learning rate, point count, and real/complex domains, which strengthens the empirical case beyond the three main benchmarks.

Good engagement with and correct positioning against prior attitude-estimation literature (Davenport, QUEST, ESOQ2, FLAE, OLAE) and prior deep rotation-learning representations (Gram-Schmidt, SVD, QCQP), with numerical validation that the new SU(2)-based Wahba solvers match optimal existing solvers.
weaknesses: Empirical gains for the proposed learning representations (2-vec, QuadMobius) over existing strong baselines (QCQP, SVD, Gram-Schmidt) are frequently marginal and inconsistent across benchmarks/scenes/categories (e.g., Table 2 Old Hospital, Table 1 Sofa), undercutting the strong claim that QuadMobius achieves "the top result in nearly all experiments."

No reported variance across multiple random seeds/training runs for the main learning benchmarks (Tables 1, 2, and the large synthetic sweep in Table 6), making it hard to assess whether the reported differences are statistically meaningful rather than noise, especially given the small margins.

QuadMobius representations are substantially more computationally expensive at both training and inference time (Table 7, roughly 2-4x slower than SVD/QCQP), which is a real practical cost that is not weighed against the marginal accuracy improvements in the main results discussion.

The paper is very heavy on dense algebraic derivations with a disproportionately long appendix (32 pages of proofs/derivations vs. 9 pages of main text), which may hurt accessibility and makes it harder for reviewers/readers to verify the many claims relative to the empirical payoff.

The baselines compared for representation learning (Gram-Schmidt 2019, SVD/QCQP 2020) are several years old; there is no comparison to more recent rotation-representation or rotation-estimation methods, leaving unclear how the proposed methods stack up against current state of the art.

The practical significance/impact of the SU(2) reformulation for the broader ML or robotics community is not strongly established beyond modest empirical improvements; the contribution is largely a mathematically elegant but incremental reframing of known Wahba's-problem machinery.

Some efficiency claims (e.g., Table 5's operation counts) are presented without full context (e.g., trade-offs between square roots, divisions, and multiplications, and lack of edge-case handling in the reported counts), making the stated efficiency advantage harder to evaluate rigorously.

strengths: The paper develops a genuinely novel theoretical framework connecting SU(2)/special unitary matrices and complex projective (stereographic) space to Wahba's problem, deriving linear constraints on quaternion parameters that unify several classical results.
The two-point (n=2) closed-form solutions are shown to be more computationally efficient than existing closed-form solvers (Table 5), which is a concrete, verifiable practical contribution.

Extensive and rigorous appendix with detailed proofs (nearest unitary matrix, weighted/unweighted two-point averaging, degenerate case handling, analytic backpropagation derivatives) demonstrates strong mathematical care.

The learning experiments span three diverse benchmarks (ModelNet10-SO3, inverse kinematics, camera pose regression) with reasonable baselines (Euler, Quat, Gram-Schmidt, QCQP, SVD), plus useful diagnostic experiments (dropout robustness, gradient-ratio and gradient-magnitude analyses) that attempt to explain why the proposed representations might work.
Analytical derivative formulas for the SVD/eigendecomposition-based maps avoid costly autodiff through complex-valued linear algebra operations, which is a useful engineering contribution.
weaknesses: The empirical gains of the flagship contributions (2-vec, QuadMobius) over existing representations (QCQP, SVD, Gram-Schmidt) are marginal and inconsistent across tables (e.g., Table 1 differences are often in the third decimal place, Table 2 shows QCQP/GS beating QuadMobius on several sub-metrics), undermining the abstract's claim that 'extensive experiments validate the effectiveness' of the new methods.

No repeated trials, confidence intervals, or statistical significance testing are reported for the learning experiments, which is especially problematic given how close the reported numbers are between competing methods.

The 'leader count' metric used in Table 6 is an unusual and somewhat ad hoc way of arguing superiority, and is sensitive to training-curve noise/cherry-picking rather than reflecting a clear, robust final-performance advantage.

QuadMobius requires a larger (16D) output and additional computational overhead (SVD or algebraic normalization, more complex backward pass) for at best modest performance gains, so the efficiency/benefit tradeoff relative to simpler SVD/QCQP maps is not clearly favorable (Table 7 shows QuadMobius is 2-3x slower in training/inference).

The core idea behind the new learning representations is fairly incremental: both essentially reinterpret/generalize existing SVD- and QCQP-style projection approaches (Levinson et al. 2020; Peretroukhin et al. 2020) through the SU(2)/Möbius lens, inheriting most of their theoretical properties rather than introducing a fundamentally different learning paradigm.

The paper is extremely dense and long (32 pages, heavy on notation and derivations), with most of the substantive theoretical content relegated to the appendix; this significantly hampers clarity and accessibility for a general audience, and the main text does not adequately motivate why the practical reader should care about the marginal empirical improvements.

Baselines are somewhat dated (2019-2020 papers); no comparison to more recent rotation-representation learning methods is included, leaving the significance of the improvement relative to current state of the art unclear.
Limitations of the proposed representations (failure modes, sensitivity to hyperparameters, when QuadMobius under/over-performs) are not discussed substantively in the main text.

strengths: The paper provides a rigorous and fairly novel theoretical framework connecting SU(2)/Möbius transformations with Wahba's problem, deriving linear constraints on quaternion parameters from multiple complementary perspectives (stereographic plane, Möbius approximation, 3D sphere).

Extensive supplementary proofs and derivations (Appendix A-F) give strong mathematical grounding and reproducibility for the theoretical claims, including derivations of gradients/backpropagation formulas needed for the proposed neural representations.

The paper translates the theory into practically useful outputs: efficient two-point closed-form solvers (with reduced multiplication counts vs. existing methods), a numerically robust degenerate-case handling scheme, and two new continuous rotation representations (2-vec and QuadMobius) for learning.

Experimental validation is broad, spanning synthetic Wahba's problem benchmarks, 3D shape pose estimation (ModelNet10-SO3), unsupervised inverse kinematics, and real-world camera pose regression (Cambridge Landmarks), with numerous baselines (Euler, Quat, Gram-Schmidt, QCQP, SVD).

Additional analysis experiments (gradient ratio distributions, dropout robustness, toy ablations of QuadMobius components) provide useful mechanistic insight into why the proposed representations may offer more stable gradients during training.
Synthetic Wahba solver validation (Table 4) confirms correctness by matching optimal classical solvers exactly, lending credibility to the derived formulas.
weaknesses: The learning experiment improvements are often marginal and inconsistent across benchmarks/categories (e.g., Tables 1-2), with QCQP/SVD frequently very close to or occasionally beating the proposed representations, making the practical significance of the gains less clear-cut.

The core theoretical contribution (SU(2)-based reformulation of Wahba's problem) mostly reproduces results numerically identical to well-established classical solvers (Table 4), suggesting the primary novel practical value lies in the derived representations/algorithms rather than fundamentally new estimation capability.

QuadMobius, despite good accuracy, is notably more computationally expensive (Table 7) and higher-dimensional (16D) than competing representations, which could limit its practical appeal despite modest accuracy gains.

The paper is extremely dense and heavily notation-laden, which may hinder accessibility and broader adoption; central claims are spread across a lengthy appendix rather than self-contained in the main text.
No explicit mention of code/artifact release is made, which could limit reproducibility of the more intricate numerical/backpropagation procedures despite detailed formulas.

Related recent alternative rotation representations (e.g., manifold gradient layers of Chen et al. 2022) are used only as training pipelines but not directly compared as representation baselines, leaving the competitive landscape only partially covered.
